title: Warmup Web Server
topicBrief: Every networked device exposes numbered ports for services such as web, email, or file transfer. Attackers may scan to see which doors are open. In this safe lesson, a fictional FTP service was mistakenly left open to anonymous visitors.
scenario: A small company's fictional web server is misconfigured. Use only this scripted terminal to understand what a security tester would notice — no command leaves this app.

tasks.prompt: Scan target.thm. Which ports are open? Enter them separated by a comma.
tasks.hint2: The simulated nmap output lists 21 and 80.

tasks.prompt: Which service is running on port 21?
Use the safe FTP transcript to find and submit the flag.
tasks.hint1: Connect with ftp target.thm, then list the files.
tasks.hint2: The final file is flag.txt; read it with cat flag.txt.

commandHints.default: That command is not part of this safe training simulation. Try nmap target.thm, ftp target.thm, ls, or cat flag.txt.

learn.title: Why anonymous FTP is risky
learn.body: Anonymous FTP lets anyone browse files without a personal account. On a real system that can expose documents by accident. Disable public access unless it is truly required, and use authenticated, modern file-transfer controls.
